title: Apply basic agricultural enterprise selection principles

lessons.title: Choosing what to farm
lessons.html:
What is an enterprise?

An enterprise is one type of farming that you do to sell or to feed your family. Examples: growing cabbages, keeping layer hens for eggs, a small herd of goats, a pig unit, growing maize, keeping bees for honey.

Choosing an enterprise is a big decision. It takes money, time and work. If you choose well, you can earn a living. If you choose badly, you can lose your money.

Questions to ask about your land

  • Rain and water – how much rain falls, and when? Is there a borehole, dam or river you may use? Vegetables need water often. Goats and cattle on veld need less.
  • Hot or cold – is there frost in winter? Frost kills crops like tomatoes, bananas and mangoes.
  • Soil – is it deep or shallow, sandy or clay? Does water drain away or stand in pools?
  • Size of land – a small plot can carry vegetables or chickens. Cattle need a lot of veld.
  • Slope – steep land is better for grazing or trees than for ploughing.

Questions to ask about yourself

  • What do you know how to do? What have you learnt?
  • How much money do you have to start?
  • How many people can help you, and how much time do you have?
  • Do you like the work? Dairy cows must be milked every day, even on Sundays.

Example

Sipho has one hectare near a small town. There is a borehole but no electricity. Winters have frost. He has some money saved and his wife can help. Cattle need too much land. Bananas will freeze. Vegetables like cabbage, spinach and onions grow well in his area and he can water them from the borehole with a hand pump or solar pump.

lessons.title: Market, money and making the choice
lessons.html:
Is there a buyer?

Never start an enterprise before you know who will buy. Ask:

  • Who will buy? Neighbours, spaza shops, hawkers, schools, a butcher, a market?
  • How much will they buy, and how often?
  • What price will they pay?
  • How far is the buyer? Who will transport the product?

Fresh vegetables, milk and eggs spoil fast, so the buyer must be close. Grain, dried beans and live animals can be kept or moved further.

Money questions

  • Start-up costs – what must you buy to begin? For example a fence, a chicken house, seed, a pump.
  • Running costs – feed, seed, fertiliser, medicine, transport, wages.
  • Time to first income – spinach can be sold in about two months. Fruit trees take years.
  • Profit – will the money from sales be more than all the costs?
  • Risk – what can go wrong? Drought, disease, theft, low prices.

Steps to choose an enterprise

  1. Make a list of enterprises that might work.
  2. Cross out those that do not suit your land, water and climate.
  3. Cross out those with no buyer nearby.
  4. Cross out those you cannot afford to start.
  5. For those left, work out costs and income, and think about the risks.
  6. Ask an extension officer or an experienced farmer for advice.
  7. Choose one and start small. Grow when you have learnt and made a profit.

Do not put all your eggs in one basket

Many small farmers have two or three enterprises, for example vegetables and chickens. If one has a bad season, the other can still bring in money. Chicken manure can also feed the vegetable garden.

Key points

  • An enterprise is one type of farming for sale or food.
  • Check rain, water, frost, soil, land size and slope.
  • Think about your skills, money, help and time.
  • Find a buyer before you start.
  • Work out costs, income and risk; start small and grow.
